label: flagship: wins all three exams
result: Final results, all solutions replay-checked. The flagship setting allows two ordinary moves before planning. Standard exam (graded, 232 puzzles): 231 solved, with 0.94 extra moves vs perfect play. The old planning language has a measured limit: 1.17 extra moves. That limit binds any planner that speaks only that vocabulary. It is a measurement, not a mathematical proof. This change went below it. A third ordinary move improves this a little more, to 0.86 extra moves (average over its own 231 solves — same solve count as depth-2). Hard exam (frontier, 218 puzzles): 177 solved, with one to two fewer moves than every alternative. New-boards exam (unseen, 200 puzzles): 188 solved, with 1.47 extra moves vs perfect on the 137 puzzles with known optima. The win repeated with two different network pairs. It also worked, unchanged, on larger boards (17 wins, 0 losses on moves) and crowded boards (23 wins, 0 losses). One caution: the rival move-by-move planner here is the original network. A re-tuned version would likely close part of the measured gap (see the project log, entry 24 — a companion document, not part of this page).
conclusion: Our flagship planner and the biggest finding of the program. Letting the planner make one or two ordinary moves before subgoal planning beats every pure-subgoal planner, everywhere we tried. A third move adds only a little. The benefit stops there.
note: Search-only change (no training); stochasticity is the search rng only. Gates: unseen moves 31/1 p=1.5e-8; graded moves 30/0 p=1.9e-9.
